subject: lighthouse
pitch: A cozy lighthouse diorama on a tiny rocky island. A red-and-white striped tower with a glowing lantern room and a black iron balcony, a keeper's cottage with a crooked chimney and a blue door, a wooden jetty with a rowboat tied to it, a couple of seagulls, tufts of grass and wildflowers between the rocks, and turquoise water with white foam around the shore, all on a round display base.

For scale, I'm deciding on proportions: a round display base roughly 2 meters wide, with the lighthouse tower standing about 3.6 meters tall, keeping everything cute and proportional rather than strictly realistic.

I'm layering the structure from the ground up — a dark plinth cylinder as the display base, a thin turquoise water disc sitting on top of it with foam detailing around the edges, and then the rocky island built up above the water.

For the foam, I'm thinking a swept tube following the irregular island shoreline at the waterline, giving it a soft white ring rather than a perfect circular band, and considering a noise-based paint for the water to add turquoise variation.

I should estimate texel density for the paint sheet given the water disc's painted area, aiming for roughly 6mm per texel, which seems adequate. For the lighthouse stripes, I need to figure out which axis parameter makes the bands ring horizontally around the tower rather than running vertically along it.

I'm reasoning that axis refers to the direction along which bands stack, so horizontal rings on a vertical tower need axis "y" -- matching the classic red/white candy-striped lighthouse look. I'm uncertain whether the size parameter represents a full period or half period, so I'll pick a reasonable value and consider an alternative explicit paint function using height modulo to alternate colors as a fallback.

Checking the paint signature and confirming stripes, spots, countershade, and paint are all exported from the package root alongside helpers like noise, cells, mix, and smoothstep.

I'll use createBuilder with the name "lighthouse-diorama", export a meta object and default build function, and start mapping out which builder methods I'll need: joint, chain, sweep, loft, part, stick, surface, extrude, lathe, and member-related calls.

I'm also considering using SVG textures for the cottage windows or door panel to add detail via a decal, while staying within the flat-color and part-count limits. Now I'm sketching the overall scene layout in meters with +Z as forward.

Mapping out the diorama: tower slightly right of center, cottage on the opposite side, a jetty with a tied rowboat extending toward the front, seagulls overhead, and grass/wildflowers scattered among rocks and water. I'm defining the circular display base as a lathe profile with a beveled brass rim, setting segments to 48 for smoother roundness despite the low-poly aesthetic elsewhere.

Now I'm working out the layered geometry for the base and water -- deciding to use around 36-40 lathe segments for a believable circular base, then nesting a water disc just inside the rim so the brass edge stays visible while the water sits slightly recessed within the top bevel.

Writing shoreline paint logic...

Now thinking about how to shape the island itself — a perfect circular lathe feels too uniform, so I'm considering a loft with irregular station widths/heights along a vertical path to create a rocky, non-circular mound instead.

The top cap being round works fine for the dome shape. I'm also weighing a lathe approach for the island instead—faceted low-poly rocks could work, but lathe gives a circular footprint, whereas I want something more irregular, which loft handles better even without lateral offset per station.

Actually, loft stations do have positional centers, so I can offset them to make the island asymmetric, though the cross-sections stay perpendicular to a near-vertical path. The trickier part is matching the loft's skin to the water surface—the island's radius where it crosses the waterline needs to align with the foam/shore radius, so I'm sketching an approximate half-width at the water level to keep the shoreline consistent rather than solving it exactly.

Trying to work out the loft cross-sections — maybe using an ellipse shape per station rather than exactly matching an irregular shore function, since lumps can't easily vary by angle. I'm considering alternatives too: closed sweeps make hollow tubes rather than solid shapes, and slabs give flat-topped sharp-edged prisms, so neither quite suits a natural island form.

Thinking through an extrude approach for a blob-shaped island with beveled edges — figuring out which plane the outline sits in and how the thickness direction gets computed from the x/y basis vectors, giving a flat-topped stone plinth look. As an alternative, I'm also considering building the island from clustered low-poly rock lumps (like dodecahedrons) scattered together for a more organic, rocky cluster effect instead of one smooth extruded shape.

Scattered dodecahedron rocks with flat shading, random scale and rotation would give that classic low-poly stylized boulder look, clustered together for an irregular shoreline with some rocks half-submerged. For the main landmass, I'll combine a lofted mound with varying station offsets for the overall lumpy shape, plus these rock boulders layered on top for detail, confirming that the loft can stay a single bone/joint since it's one continuous mesh.
